issues.explanation: For stalking trauma, 'Betrayal' can be plausible if the stalker was known to the patient, but the profile provides no supporting items suggesting an interpersonal betrayal context. More importantly, 'Contamination' is typically associated with sexual assault or physical violation and is hard to reconcile clinically with stalking in the absence of any other items indicating assault, bodily intrusion, or abuse.

Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Contamination' point to different trauma meanings: interpersonal trust violation versus bodily violation. They can coexist in some cases, but with stalking alone and no corroborating memory, trigger, or threat items, this combination is clinically difficult to justify.

For stalking trauma, 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is hard to reconcile unless there was an additional sexual or physical assault element. On its face, this appraisal is clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

'Avoid Medical Care' implies avoidance centered on trauma-related examination, disclosure, or bodily injury/assault concerns, but there are no Memory, Threat, or Trigger items indicating injury, assault, or medical trauma. It is poorly matched to the rest of this stalking profile.

vignette:
Leilani was twenty years old, a senior accounting student who had just started working as an auditor at a mid-sized firm in Honolulu. Her trauma had begun quietly, almost imperceptibly, a year earlier during her sophomore year. A classmate in her statistics course, a man named Derek, had started sitting next to her every lecture, then waiting for her outside the building, then sending her long, detailed messages about her daily schedule. She had politely declined his invitations for coffee, but he had not stopped. Over six months, it escalated into a relentless pattern: he appeared at the library carrel she favored, at the coffee shop she visited after class, and once, memorably, at the bus stop she used at 6:15 p.m. every Tuesday. The final incident that made her file a police report involved him following her all the way to her apartment, standing outside her door for forty-five minutes, whispering her name through the wood while she sat frozen on the floor, phone clutched in her hand, too afraid to call out.

In the months that followed, Leilani's world contracted. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, a conviction that had settled into her bones like a low-grade fever. Every stranger on the street, every car that slowed near her, every unexpected notification on her phone felt like a potential threat. This belief shaped everything she did. She told herself she had to be on guard all the time, and she meant it literally: she scanned parking lots before exiting her car, checked the back seat through the window, and memorized the faces of everyone within twenty feet of her cubicle at work. Her job as an auditor required her to verify financial records at several different client sites around the city, a task that now felt like a series of gauntlets. Each new office building meant a new parking garage, a new lobby, a new set of hallways where anyone could be watching.

Because the world felt so dangerous, Leilani had developed a set of strategies that made sense to her in the moment but were slowly dismantling her life. She began avoiding going out altogether after work, declining every invitation from colleagues and friends. She told herself it was safer to stay home, but the truth was more complicated: she had also begun to feel that she deserved to suffer because of what had happened. She would catch herself thinking that if she hadn't worn that particular dress to class, or if she hadn't smiled when Derek first said hello, none of this would have happened. This punishment thinking had become a quiet, persistent voice that she did not challenge. She also actively avoided situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful, because hope felt dangerous-it made her feel exposed, as though happiness was something that could be taken from her again. Her colleagues noticed her withdrawal and stopped inviting her to team lunches. Her supervisor mentioned that her performance had slipped slightly, that she seemed distracted during client meetings. Leilani knew this was true. She was distracted. She was always watching the door.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago. She was reviewing a client's expense reports in a small conference room on the third floor when a maintenance worker knocked on the glass door to ask about a light fixture. She had not heard him approach. The knock sent her heart into her throat, and she had scrambled backward, knocking over her chair, before she realized who he was. The humiliation of that moment-her own fear, the man's startled apology, the way her hands had trembled for the next hour-had made her realize she could not continue like this. She was afraid of what she was becoming: a woman who flinched at a knock, who had stopped answering her phone, who had not felt a moment of genuine lightness in nearly a year. She wanted that back. She was terrified she never would.
